derivations.claim: For each initial state $i$, choose a shortest path in [A1] to a state with positive escape probability. A shortest path has no repeated state, since deleting the segment between two repetitions leaves a shorter path with the same endpoint; hence it uses at most $n-1$ transitions. The probability of following that path and then escaping is $p_i=(\prod_{r<k}T_{i_r i_{r+1}})d_{i_k}>0$, where the empty product is $1$. The finitely many choices are made by induction over the finite state set.

Let $L=n$ and $\varepsilon=\min_i p_i$. A finite minimum of positive reals is positive, and every row loses at least $p_i\ge\varepsilon$ mass by step $L$, so $T^L\mathbf 1\le(1-\varepsilon)\mathbf 1$.

Since $T\mathbf 1\le\mathbf 1$, induction gives $T^r\mathbf 1\le\mathbf 1$ for $0\le r<L$. For $k=aL+r$, nonnegativity and step 2.1 give $T^k\mathbf 1=(T^L)^aT^r\mathbf 1\le(1-\varepsilon)^a\mathbf 1$. Thus $\|T^k\|_\infty\le(1-\varepsilon)^a$ and $T^k\to0$.

For any $v\in\mathbb C^n$, step 2.1 gives $\|T^Lv\|_\infty\le(1-\varepsilon)\|v\|_\infty$, by bounding each row sum of absolute values with the corresponding row sum of $T^L$. If $Tv=\lambda v$ with $v\ne0$, then $|\lambda|^L\|v\|_\infty=\|T^Lv\|_\infty\le(1-\varepsilon)\|v\|_\infty$, so $|\lambda|\le(1-\varepsilon)^{1/L}<1$. Thus $\rho(T)<1$.

Let $S=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with $n\ge1$. A matrix $P=(P_{ij})_{i,j\in S}$ is **column-stochastic** when $P_{ij}\ge0$ and $\sum_{i\in S}P_{ij}=1$ for every source index $j$. A **column probability vector** is $x\in\mathbb R^n$ with $x_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i x_i=1$. A **stationary probability vector** for $P$ is a column probability vector $\pi$ satisfying $P\pi=\pi$. For $z\in\mathbb R^n$, write $\|z\|_1=\sum_i|z_i|$ and $H=\{z:\sum_i z_i=0\}$.

The published transition-matrix convention [[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]] is row-stochastic: its row index is the source and its column index the destination. If $K$ is such a matrix, then $P=K^{\mathsf T}$ is column-stochastic; a row law $u$ updated by $uK$ corresponds to the column law $u^{\mathsf T}$ updated by $P u^{\mathsf T}$. All displays on this page that use $Px$ or $Qx$ use this column convention.

derivations.claim: For every $z$, finite summation and [F1] give $\sum_i(Pz)_i=\sum_j(\sum_iP_{ij})z_j=\sum_jz_j$. If $z$ is a column probability vector, each coordinate of $Pz$ is a sum of nonnegative terms, so $Pz\ge0$ and its coordinate sum is one.
For each row $i$, $|(Pz)_i|=|\sum_jP_{ij}z_j|\le\sum_jP_{ij}|z_j|$ because $P_{ij}\ge0$. Summing over $i$ and regrouping finite sums gives $\|Pz\|_1\le\sum_j|z_j|\sum_iP_{ij}=\|z\|_1$.

derivations.claim: Let $z\in H$ with $\|z\|_1=1$. Write $z=z^+-z^-$ coordinatewise, where $z_i^+=\max(z_i,0)$ and $z_i^- =\max(-z_i,0)$. Since $\sum_i z_i=0$, the positive and negative masses agree, and their sum is one; hence $\sum_i z_i^+=\sum_i z_i^-=1/2$. Therefore $u=2z^+$ and $v=2z^-$ are probability vectors and $Pz=(Pu-Pv)/2$.

We have $Pu=\sum_j u_jp_j$ and $Pv=\sum_kv_kp_k$. Thus $Pz=\frac12\sum_{j,k}u_jv_k(p_j-p_k)$. The coefficients $u_jv_k$ are nonnegative and sum to one, so the triangle inequality gives $\|Pz\|_1\le\frac12\max_{j,k}\|p_j-p_k\|_1$. Taking the supremum over such $z$ proves the upper bound.

If $n\ge2$ and the maximum is positive, a maximizing pair has $j\ne k$; if the maximum is zero, any distinct pair maximizes it. Choose such a distinct pair and set $z=(e_j-e_k)/2$. Then $z\in H$, $\|z\|_1=1$, and $Pz=(p_j-p_k)/2$, so the supremum is at least $\frac12\max_{j,k}\|p_j-p_k\|_1$. If $n=1$, both sides are zero by definition. This proves the first equality.

For two nonnegative probability columns $a,b$, $|a_i-b_i|=a_i+b_i-2\min(a_i,b_i)$. Summing gives $\frac12\|a-b\|_1=1-\sum_i\min(a_i,b_i)$. Apply this to every pair of columns; taking the maximum of the left side is one minus the minimum overlap on the right.

If $n\ge2$, [F2] bounds every norm in the defining supremum by one, so $0\le\delta(P)\le1$; if $n=1$, $\delta(P)=0$ by definition. For nonzero $z\in H$, apply the definition of $\delta(P)$ to $z/\|z\|_1$ and use homogeneity; for $z=0$ the inequality is immediate. Thus $\|Pz\|_1\le\delta(P)\|z\|_1$ on all of $H$.

Let $E$ be countable with sigma-algebra $2^E$, and let $K$ be a probability kernel on it. For $x,y\in E$, set

$$p(x,y):=K(x,\{y\}),\qquad p^{(n)}(x,y):=K^n(x,\{y\})\quad(n\in\mathbb N_0),$$

where $K^0$ is the identity kernel, so $p^{(0)}(x,y)=\mathbf 1_{\{x=y\}}$. By [[def-iterated-transition-kernels]], each $K^n$ is a probability kernel. Since measures on countable discrete spaces are their singleton-weighted sums ([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), every row satisfies

$$\sum_{y\in E}p^{(n)}(x,y)=K^n(x,E)=1.$$

No conditional-expectation version or choice function is used in this matrix definition.

Let $T\in[0,\infty)^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, have row sums at most one. Define the one-step escape probability $d_i=1-\sum_jT_{ij}$. Suppose that for each state $i$ there is a path $i=i_0,i_1,\ldots,i_k$ with $T_{i_r i_{r+1}}>0$ for $0\le r<k$ and $d_{i_k}>0$. Then there are $L\le n$ and $\varepsilon>0$ such that $T^L\mathbf 1\le(1-\varepsilon)\mathbf 1$. Writing $k=aL+r$ with $0\le r<L$ gives $\|T^k\|_\infty\le(1-\varepsilon)^a$, so $T^k\to0$. In particular, every complex eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $T$ satisfies $|\lambda|<1$, and its spectral radius $\rho(T):=\max\{|\lambda|:\det(\lambda I-T)=0\}$ is less than one.

derivations.claim: For $0\le r<L$, substochasticity gives $T^r\mathbf 1\le\mathbf 1$. Since $T^L\mathbf 1\le(1-\varepsilon)\mathbf 1$, induction gives $(T^L)^q\mathbf 1\le(1-\varepsilon)^q\mathbf 1$ for every $q\ge0$. Therefore every row sum of $T^{qL+r}$ is at most $(1-\varepsilon)^q$, and $\sum_{k\ge0}\|T^k\|_\infty\le L\sum_{q\ge0}(1-\varepsilon)^q=L/\varepsilon$.

The series $N=\sum_{k\ge0}T^k$ converges in the maximum-row-sum norm and has nonnegative entries. The finite partial sums satisfy $(I-T)\sum_{k=0}^{m}T^k=I-T^{m+1}$ and $\sum_{k=0}^{m}T^k(I-T)=I-T^{m+1}$. Step 1.1 makes $T^{m+1}\to0$, so $N$ is a two-sided inverse of $I-T$ and $\|N\|_\infty\le L/\varepsilon$.

Put $d=\mathbf1-T\mathbf1$, the vector of one-step exit weights from rows of $U$. For each $i$, the total weight of first-exit paths of length at most $N$ is $\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(T^kd)_i=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(T^k\mathbf1-T^{k+1}\mathbf1)_i=1-(T^N\mathbf1)_i$. By [F2], this tends to one. The finite-exit path set is countable, so these nonnegative weights define a probability distribution. For paths exiting into $G$ after $k$ transitions within $U$, finite matrix multiplication gives weight $(T^kb)_i$; summing over $k$ yields $h_i=\sum_{k\ge0}(T^kb)_i=(Nb)_i$.

For a path with exit length $\tau$, the indicator identity $\tau=\sum_{k\ge0}\mathbf1_{\{\tau>k\}}$ holds. Summing against the countable path probability from step 2.2 gives $\mathbb E_i\tau=\sum_{k\ge0}\Pr_i(\tau>k)$, since both are the same nonnegative double sum indexed by pairs $0\le k<\tau$. The total weight of paths still in $U$ after $k$ transitions is $(T^k\mathbf1)_i$, so $t_i=\sum_{k\ge0}(T^k\mathbf1)_i=(N\mathbf1)_i$. Step 1.1 makes this finite, and multiplying by $I-T$ gives $(I-T)t=\mathbf1$.

From $h-\widehat h=N\bigl(b-(I-T)\widehat h\bigr)$, the operator norm bound in step 2.1 gives the stated hitting-probability residual bound. Applying the same identity to $t-\widehat t$ with right side $\mathbf 1$ gives the mean-exit residual bound.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

([[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]), that is,
some probability vector $\pi$ on $E$ satisfies $\pi p=\pi$. No irreducibility,
aperiodicity or recurrence hypothesis is needed, and the argument uses no
choice principle and no Markov-chain path law.

Let $E$ be countable with sigma-algebra $2^E$, and let $K$ be a probability kernel on it. For $x,y\in E$, set

$$p(x,y):=K(x,\{y\}),\qquad p^{(n)}(x,y):=K^n(x,\{y\})\quad(n\in\mathbb N_0),$$

where $K^0$ is the identity kernel, so $p^{(0)}(x,y)=\mathbf 1_{\{x=y\}}$. By [[def-iterated-transition-kernels]], each $K^n$ is a probability kernel. Since measures on countable discrete spaces are their singleton-weighted sums ([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), every row satisfies

$$\sum_{y\in E}p^{(n)}(x,y)=K^n(x,E)=1.$$

No conditional-expectation version or choice function is used in this matrix definition.

**Graph convention.** For any finite real column-stochastic matrix $P$ on $S=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, the positive-transition graph has a directed edge $j\to i$ exactly when $P_{ij}>0$. This defines the communicating classes and closed classes for real matrices, whether or not their entries can be computed exactly.

**Algorithm input.** An exact finite real matrix $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ with indexed state set $S=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and $n\ge1$, represented in an exact arithmetic model that terminates on the required comparisons with zero. If an entry is negative or any column sum differs from one, return `invalid-input`. Rational entries provide an effective instance of this exact-comparison interface. A rounded input without certified sign and column-sum decisions is outside this procedure's input contract.

**Output.** A partition of $S$ into the strongly connected components of the directed graph of positive transitions, the list of closed communicating classes, and the remaining transient states.

**Procedure.** Form the usual row-transition matrix $K=P^{\mathsf T}$. Initialize a Boolean relation $R_{ij}$ to true exactly when $i=j$ or $K_{ij}>0$. For $k=1,\ldots,n$, and then for every $i,j$, replace $R_{ij}$ by $R_{ij}\lor(R_{ik}\land R_{kj})$. Place $i,j$ in the same component exactly when both $R_{ij}$ and $R_{ji}$ are true. Mark a component $C$ closed exactly when $K_{ij}=0$ for every $i\in C$ and $j\notin C$. Return the closed components, the nonclosed components, and their state labels in increasing order. The procedure uses finitely many exact comparisons and Boolean updates; no sparse storage format or cost bound is asserted. It is a graph computation under the exact-comparison interface, not a claim that positivity of arbitrary unrepresented real numbers can be decided from rounded approximations.

Let $T\in[0,\infty)^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, have row sums at most one. Define the one-step escape probability $d_i=1-\sum_jT_{ij}$. Suppose that for each state $i$ there is a path $i=i_0,i_1,\ldots,i_k$ with $T_{i_r i_{r+1}}>0$ for $0\le r<k$ and $d_{i_k}>0$. Then there are $L\le n$ and $\varepsilon>0$ such that $T^L\mathbf 1\le(1-\varepsilon)\mathbf 1$. Writing $k=aL+r$ with $0\le r<L$ gives $\|T^k\|_\infty\le(1-\varepsilon)^a$, so $T^k\to0$. In particular, every complex eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $T$ satisfies $|\lambda|<1$, and its spectral radius $\rho(T):=\max\{|\lambda|:\det(\lambda I-T)=0\}$ is less than one.

Suppose $T$ satisfies the escape hypothesis of [[lem-finite-transient-block-geometric-escape]] with constants $L\le |U|$ and $\varepsilon>0$. For each $i\in U$, give a finite first-exit path $(i=i_0,i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$, with $i_0,\ldots,i_k\in U$ and $j\in U^c$, the weight $\prod_{r<k}K_{i_r i_{r+1}}\,K_{i_kj}$. The proof shows these countably many path weights sum to one, so they define a probability distribution on finite first-exit paths. Let $G\subseteq U^c$, set $b_i=\sum_{j\in G}K_{ij}$, and let $h_i$ be the probability that the path exits into $G$; let $t_i$ be the mean number of transitions to exit. $$\|N\|_\infty\le L/\varepsilon,\qquad \|h-\widehat h\|_\infty\le(L/\varepsilon)\|b-(I-T)\widehat h\|_\infty,$$

where $h_i$ is the probability that the first exit from $U$ lands in $G$ and $h=Nb$. The expected number $t_i$ of steps until the first exit from $U$ is finite and satisfies $t=N\mathbf 1$; for any $\widehat t$,

$$\|t-\widehat t\|_\infty\le(L/\varepsilon)\|\mathbf 1-(I-T)\widehat t\|_\infty.$$

Thus these hitting and mean-exit systems are certified only for a proved transient block; a row-substochastic matrix without the escape hypothesis receives no such conclusion here. The matrix norm is $\|A\|_\infty=\max_i\sum_j|A_{ij}|$ and the vector norm is $\|v\|_\infty=\max_i|v_i|$.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give

measures evaluated at $A$.

$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see

([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

derivations.claim: The finite graph's strongly connected components form a partition, and its component graph has no directed cycle: a cycle would make its components mutually reachable and hence one component. Following outgoing edges from any component must therefore terminate at a sink, since the component graph is finite and acyclic. A sink is exactly a closed component by [F2]. From any state outside the closed classes, follow a component path to a sink. Each component edge is realized by a positive transition, and strong connectivity supplies finite positive paths from the current state to the source of each such transition and from its endpoint to the next transition's source. Concatenating these paths gives a positive-transition path into a closed class. Before its first entry, this path stays in U because a closed class has no outgoing edge. If U is nonempty, [F3] applies to T. Writing k=aL+r as in [F3] gives $\|T^k\|_\infty\to0$, so the Neumann series $N=\sum_{k\ge0}T^k$ converges and is $(I-T)^{-1}$.

For each closed class $C_j$, the restriction $K_{C_j,C_j}$ is a finite irreducible row-stochastic matrix. By [F5] it has a unique invariant probability $\pi_j$. Extending $\pi_j$ by zero outside $C_j$ preserves invariance because no transition leaves the class. Thus every convex combination in the statement is invariant.

Let $v$ be any invariant probability row vector and write its coordinates as $(v_C,v_U)$. Since closed classes have no transitions to U, the stationary equation on the transient coordinates is $v_U=v_UT$. If U is nonempty, [F3] gives $T^L\mathbf 1\le(1-\varepsilon)\mathbf 1$ for some $\varepsilon>0$, and therefore $\|v_U\|_1=\|v_UT^L\|_1\le\sum_{i\in U}(v_U)_i\sum_{k\in U}(T^L)_{ik}\le(1-\varepsilon)\|v_U\|_1$. Hence $v_U=0$. Since no closed class has transitions to another closed class, the stationary equation now restricts separately to each block $C_j$. Thus each $v_{C_j}$ is invariant on its class, so [F5] makes it $\alpha_j\pi_j$ with $\alpha_j\ge0$; their masses sum to one. This proves the asserted full set of invariant probabilities.

For each transient state i, the probability weight of first entering class $C_j$ after k transient transitions is $(e_i^{\mathsf T}T^kb_j)$. These disjoint first-entry weights sum, by [F4], to $((I-T)^{-1}b_j)_i$. Initial mass already in $C_j$ remains there, so the total class weight from u is $\alpha_j=u(C_j)+u_U(I-T)^{-1}b_j$. Moreover $\sum_jb_j=(I-T)\mathbf 1$, since every transition from a transient state either remains in U or enters exactly one of the closed classes; thus $\sum_j\alpha_j=u(C_1\cup\cdots\cup C_s)+u_U\mathbf 1=1$. If U is empty, the same formula reduces directly to $u(C_j)$.

Define $\bar u_N=N^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}uK^k$. Every coordinate lies in [0,1]. From any subsequence, apply [F7] to its first coordinate, restrict to that subsequence, and repeat for the finitely many remaining coordinates; the final subsequence converges coordinatewise. Also $\bar u_NK-\bar u_N=(uK^N-u)/N$, whose ℓ1 norm is at most $2/N$. Hence every subsequential limit is an invariant probability.

The mass $a_n=uK^n(C_j)$ is nondecreasing because $C_j$ is closed; its increment at each step is the first-entry weight from step 1.4. The partial sums of these weights tend to $u_U(I-T)^{-1}b_j$ by [F3]–[F4], and the unabsorbed transient mass tends to zero, so $a_n\to\alpha_j$. Since η is arbitrary, the Cesàro class mass tends to αⱼ. Thus every subsequential limit $\bar u$ has $\bar u(C_j)=\alpha_j$ for each j. By step 1.3 this invariant probability must be $\sum_j\alpha_j\pi_j$.

A **column probability vector** is $x\in\mathbb R^n$ with $x_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i x_i=1$. A **stationary probability vector** for $P$ is a column probability vector $\pi$ satisfying $P\pi=\pi$. For $z\in\mathbb R^n$, write $\|z\|_1=\sum_i|z_i|$ and $H=\{z:\sum_i z_i=0\}$.

If $K$ is such a matrix, then $P=K^{\mathsf T}$ is column-stochastic; a row law $u$ updated by $uK$ corresponds to the column law $u^{\mathsf T}$ updated by $P u^{\mathsf T}$. This defines the communicating classes and closed classes for real matrices, whether or not their entries can be computed exactly.

Let $S=\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}$ with $n\ge1$. Identify its real matrices with $M_n(\mathbb R)$, the finite matrix space with row and column indices in $S$ from [[def-matrix-space]], and use the matrix-product and identity conventions of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. A **finite column generator** on $S$ is a real matrix $Q=(q_{ij})\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ satisfying

$$q_{ij}\ge0\quad(i\ne j),\qquad \sum_{i<n}q_{ij}=0\quad(j<n).$$

The column index $j$ is the source state and the row index $i$ is the destination state: for $i\ne j$, $q_{ij}$ is the transition rate from $j$ to $i$. The exit rate from $j$ is

$$r_j:=-q_{jj}=\sum_{i\ne j}q_{ij}\ge0.$$

A **column probability vector** is $p\in\mathbb R^n$ with $p_i\ge0$ for each $i$ and $\sum_{i<n}p_i=1$. A **subprobability vector** has the same coordinatewise nonnegativity and has coordinate sum at most one. These conventions are used throughout this page.

**Inputs.** An integer $n\ge1$, an exact rational matrix $P\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}$, an exact rational raw candidate $y\in\mathbb Q^n$, and an integer $m\ge1$. The represented rational entries are the exact data for this certificate; certification proceeds only when P is column-stochastic, as checked in the first instruction.

**Outputs.** Return `invalid-input` if P has a negative entry or a column not summing exactly to one. Set $y_i^+=\max(y_i,0)$ and $s=\sum_i y_i^+$. If $s=0$, return `candidate-unavailable`. Otherwise set $x=y^+/s$ and $c=\|y-x\|_1$. Compute $M=P^m$ by $M_0=I$ and $M_{k+1}=PM_k$ for $0\le k<m$. Compute $r=Px-x$ and

$$q=1-\min_{j,k}\sum_i\min(M_{ij},M_{ik}).$$

If $q\ge1$, return `certificate-unavailable` with the corrected candidate and computed quantities; do not report an accuracy bound. If $q<1$, return `certified` with the candidate $x$, correction ledger $c$, residual $r$, coefficient $q$, and bound

$$B=c+\frac{m\|r\|_1}{1-q}.$$

All operations above use exact rational arithmetic and finitely many loops. If $q\ge1$, the procedure reports no accuracy bound; if $q<1$, it returns the stated exact bound. The procedure takes $y$ as input and makes no claim about how a stationary solver produced it.

Let $Q$ be a finite column generator, let $\nu>0$ satisfy $\nu\ge\max_j r_j$, and put $P=I+Q/\nu$. Let $m\ge1$ and $q=\delta(P^m)<1$. Then the finite master equation $p'=Qp$ has a unique stationary probability $\pi$, characterized among column probability vectors by $Q\pi=0$. For any raw vector $y\in\mathbb R^n$ and column probability vector $x$, set $c=\|y-x\|_1$. Then

$$\|y-\pi\|_1\le c+\frac{m\|Qx\|_1}{\nu(1-q)}.$$

The identity $Qx/\nu=Px-x$ makes the generator residual directly usable by the discrete certificate. In the exact algorithm branch, $y^+=0$ returns `candidate-unavailable`, and $q\ge1$ returns `certificate-unavailable`; neither status supplies an algorithmic accuracy certificate.

In particular, when P and y are rational and the exact branch of [[alg-corrected-stationary-residual-certificate]] returns `certified` with candidate x and correction c, those outputs satisfy the conditions above.

Let $p$ be a transition matrix on a countable state space $E$
([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]), and let
$\mu:E\to[0,+\infty)$ be a state measure with $\mu(x)<+\infty$ for every
$x\in E$ that satisfies detailed balance for $p$
([[def-reversible-measure-and-detailed-balance]]). Write

$$(\mu p)(y):=\sum_{x\in E}\mu(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad(y\in E),$$

the measure-matrix product, a sum of nonnegative terms in $[0,+\infty]$. Then

$$\mu p=\mu,\qquad\text{that is}\qquad(\mu p)(y)=\mu(y)\ \text{ for every }y\in E .$$

In particular the conclusion holds for a reversible state measure of infinite
total mass $\sum_{x\in E}\mu(x)=+\infty$; and if the mass is one, $\mu$ is an
invariant (equivalently stationary) probability distribution for $p$ in the
sense of [[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]].

Let $S=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with $n\ge1$. A matrix $P=(P_{ij})_{i,j\in S}$ is **column-stochastic** when $P_{ij}\ge0$ and $\sum_{i\in S}P_{ij}=1$ for every source index $j$. A **column probability vector** is $x\in\mathbb R^n$ with $x_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i x_i=1$. A **stationary probability vector** for $P$ is a column probability vector $\pi$ satisfying $P\pi=\pi$. For $z\in\mathbb R^n$, write $\|z\|_1=\sum_i|z_i|$ and $H=\{z:\sum_i z_i=0\}$.

The published transition-matrix convention [[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]] is row-stochastic: its row index is the source and its column index the destination. If $K$ is such a matrix, then $P=K^{\mathsf T}$ is column-stochastic; a row law $u$ updated by $uK$ corresponds to the column law $u^{\mathsf T}$ updated by $P u^{\mathsf T}$. All displays on this page that use $Px$ or $Qx$ use this column convention.

**Graph convention.** For any finite real column-stochastic matrix $P$ on $S=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, the positive-transition graph has a directed edge $j\to i$ exactly when $P_{ij}>0$. This defines the communicating classes and closed classes for real matrices, whether or not their entries can be computed exactly.

**Algorithm input.** An exact finite real matrix $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ with indexed state set $S=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and $n\ge1$, represented in an exact arithmetic model that terminates on the required comparisons with zero. If an entry is negative or any column sum differs from one, return `invalid-input`. Rational entries provide an effective instance of this exact-comparison interface. A rounded input without certified sign and column-sum decisions is outside this procedure's input contract.

**Output.** A partition of $S$ into the strongly connected components of the directed graph of positive transitions, the list of closed communicating classes, and the remaining transient states.

**Procedure.** Form the usual row-transition matrix $K=P^{\mathsf T}$. Initialize a Boolean relation $R_{ij}$ to true exactly when $i=j$ or $K_{ij}>0$. For $k=1,\ldots,n$, and then for every $i,j$, replace $R_{ij}$ by $R_{ij}\lor(R_{ik}\land R_{kj})$. Place $i,j$ in the same component exactly when both $R_{ij}$ and $R_{ji}$ are true. Mark a component $C$ closed exactly when $K_{ij}=0$ for every $i\in C$ and $j\notin C$. Return the closed components, the nonclosed components, and their state labels in increasing order. The procedure uses finitely many exact comparisons and Boolean updates; no sparse storage format or cost bound is asserted. It is a graph computation under the exact-comparison interface, not a claim that positivity of arbitrary unrepresented real numbers can be decided from rounded approximations.

Let $T\in[0,\infty)^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, have row sums at most one. Define the one-step escape probability $d_i=1-\sum_jT_{ij}$. Suppose that for each state $i$ there is a path $i=i_0,i_1,\ldots,i_k$ with $T_{i_r i_{r+1}}>0$ for $0\le r<k$ and $d_{i_k}>0$. Then there are $L\le n$ and $\varepsilon>0$ such that $T^L\mathbf 1\le(1-\varepsilon)\mathbf 1$. Writing $k=aL+r$ with $0\le r<L$ gives $\|T^k\|_\infty\le(1-\varepsilon)^a$, so $T^k\to0$. In particular, every complex eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $T$ satisfies $|\lambda|<1$, and its spectral radius $\rho(T):=\max\{|\lambda|:\det(\lambda I-T)=0\}$ is less than one.

derivations.claim: Before processing vertex $k$, the Boolean relation records exactly the positive paths whose intermediate vertices lie among $1,\ldots,k-1$: this is true initially because the relation contains precisely zero-step paths and one-edge paths. A path with intermediate vertices among $1,\ldots,k$ either avoids $k$, or can have repeated visits to $k$ removed and be split at its single remaining visit into two paths whose intermediate vertices are among $1,\ldots,k-1$. Conversely, concatenating those two paths gives a path through $k$. Thus the update $R_{ij}\gets R_{ij}\lor(R_{ik}\land R_{kj})$ gives exactly the reachability relation after processing $k$. The three loops range over the finite set $S$ and all required comparisons terminate by hypothesis, so the algorithm terminates.

After $k=n$, $R_{ij}$ holds exactly when $j$ is reachable from $i$. Mutual reachability is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive by zero-step paths, reversal of the two reachability assertions, and path concatenation, respectively; hence the algorithm's grouping is exactly the strongly connected component partition. Its finite scan marks a component closed exactly when there is no edge from one of its vertices to a vertex outside it, which is precisely the definition of a closed component.

The directed graph obtained by contracting each strongly connected component is finite and has no directed cycle, since a cycle would make its components mutually reachable and therefore a single component. Starting from any component and following outgoing edges must therefore reach a sink after finitely many steps; sinks are exactly the closed components from step 2.1. Lift this component path to a state path by joining each consecutive pair of intercomponent-edge endpoints with a path inside the current strongly connected component. All edges on the resulting finite state path have positive transition probabilities. A path from a nonclosed component cannot enter a closed component and later leave it, so before its first entry into a closed class it stays in $U$. Therefore every state in $U$ has a positive path through $U$ to a row with positive escape probability into a closed class.

The block $T=K_{U,U}$ is nonnegative and row-substochastic because each row of $K$ sums to one. For every row reached at the end of the path in step 3.1, the positive transition into a closed class is omitted from $T$, so its escape probability $1-\sum_{j\in U}T_{ij}$ is positive. Thus every state of $U$ satisfies the path hypothesis of [F3], which gives the claimed finite-step escape bound and geometric decay. If $U=\varnothing$, there is no transient remainder and the same output description holds without a block $T$.
